content: Beedi, also referred to as bidi or biri, is a type of thin cigarette originating from South Asia. It is crafted using tobacco that is wrapped in a tendu leaf (scientifically known as Diospyros melanoxylon) and secured at one end with colored thread. Beedis are often flavored and are smaller in size compared to conventional cigarettes. However, they produce significantly higher levels of harmful substances, including three times more carbon monoxide and nicotine, and five times more tar than regular cigarettes. The tobacco content in beedis ranges from 10% to 20%. Unlike conventional cigarettes, beedis do not contain added chemicals. Despite this, like all tobacco products, their use is associated with an increased risk of developing various types of cancer. The production of beedis is a cottage industry in India, predominantly carried out by women in their homes. The process of rolling a beedi is similar to that of making a handmade cigarette. Due to their relatively low cost compared to regular cigarettes, beedis have long been popular among economically disadvantaged populations in countries such as Bangladesh, Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Cambodia, and India. In India alone, approximately 850 billion beedis are smoked annually. Outside of South Asia, beedis are available in a variety of fruity flavors, such as vanilla, strawberry, chocolate, and mango. In Indian food markets abroad, their sale often goes unnoticed by authorities due to the markets' focus on ethnic clientele and their emphasis on food, drink, and provisions, while typically excluding alcohol products. A 1999 survey conducted by the Booker T. Washington Community Service Center in San Francisco revealed that 58% of high school students in the city had tried beedis, and 31% reported smoking them at least once a month. Alarmingly, 70% of the beedi packs purchased lacked warning labels, and around 40% did not have tax-paid stamps, contributing to their affordability. Many students who have tried beedis perceive them to be less harmful than regular cigarettes, likely due to the ease of inhalation and the absence of warning labels on the packaging.
